Neurophysiology

The brain is one of the most hormonally sensitive organs in the body.

Book an appointment Neurological health →
Clinically reviewed by Dr Gina Schoeman · Harley Street & Wimbledon · CQC registered
Overview Symptoms Diagnosis Treatment Why us Questions Book
Overview

The Relationship Between Hormones and Brain Function

The brain is one of the most hormonally sensitive organs in the body. Oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone, cortisol, and thyroid hormones all exert direct and measurable effects on neurotransmitter production, synaptic plasticity, inflammatory regulation, cerebral blood flow, and cognitive performance. When these hormones fluctuate or decline, the neurological consequences can be profound, and they are frequently the most distressing and life-disrupting dimension of hormonal change.

Neurophysiology and Hormonal Brain Health at The Schoeman Clinic addresses the intersection of hormonal medicine and brain function. This is not a psychiatric service, nor is it a standard neurology referral. It is a specialist clinical programme that investigates the hormonal, metabolic, inflammatory, and nutritional factors that drive cognitive and neurological symptoms, and that develops personalised treatment plans to restore brain health from the inside out.

Many of the patients who come to us with concerns about concentration, memory, mood, cognitive performance, or neurological symptoms have never had a hormonal assessment. The hormonal dimension of brain health is consistently underrepresented in standard clinical investigation, and the consequences of that gap are borne by the patients who receive years of inadequate or misdirected treatment as a result.

Symptoms

Conditions and Symptoms Addressed

  1. 01

    Hormonal Brain Fog and Cognitive Decline

    Brain fog, the term most commonly used by patients to describe a cluster of cognitive symptoms including impaired concentration, slowed processing, poor working memory, and a persistent sense of mental haziness, is one of the most frequently reported complaints in hormonally mediated conditions. It is a direct neurological consequence of oestrogen fluctuation in perimenopause and menopause, of thyroid hormone insufficiency, of elevated cortisol, of insulin resistance, and of nutritional deficiencies that impair neurotransmitter synthesis and neuronal energy metabolism.

    Brain fog is not a vague or trivial complaint. It represents measurable cognitive impairment that significantly affects professional performance, personal relationships, and quality of life, and it is amenable to treatment once its underlying drivers are identified and addressed.

  2. 02

    ADHD-Like Presentations in Perimenopause and Menopause

    One of the most clinically significant and underrecognised neurological phenomena associated with female hormonal transition is the emergence or dramatic worsening of attention difficulties, impulsivity, and executive dysfunction in women approaching or navigating perimenopause and menopause. Oestrogen modulates dopamine signalling, which is central to attention, focus, and impulse regulation. As oestrogen levels become erratic and ultimately decline, dopaminergic function is disrupted, producing symptoms that are functionally indistinguishable from attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

    Many women in this situation receive a new ADHD diagnosis in their forties or fifties and are commenced on stimulant medication, without any consideration of whether hormonal optimisation might substantially resolve or reduce the severity of their attention difficulties. At The Schoeman Clinic, we assess the hormonal substrate of attention and cognitive symptoms in detail before attributing them to neurodevelopmental causes alone.

    Where formal neurodevelopmental assessment for ADHD or autism is required, we refer to our specialist partner Dr Niraj Singh, a Neurodevelopmental Psychiatrist with particular expertise in neurodiversity.

  3. 03

    Hormonal Influence on Mood and Emotional Regulation

    Low mood, anxiety, emotional dysregulation, and a diminished capacity for stress tolerance are common presentations in patients with hormonal imbalance. These symptoms have a direct neurobiological basis, reflecting the effects of declining or dysregulated oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone, and cortisol on serotonin, GABA, and dopamine systems.

    Patients presenting with mood symptoms at The Schoeman Clinic receive a comprehensive hormonal assessment before any assumption is made that the cause is purely psychiatric. In many cases, effective hormonal treatment produces substantial and rapid improvement in mood and emotional resilience, reducing or eliminating the need for psychotropic medication.

  4. 04

    Neuroinflammation and Brain Health

    Chronic systemic inflammation does not remain confined to the periphery. Inflammatory mediators cross the blood-brain barrier and contribute directly to neurological symptoms including fatigue, low mood, cognitive slowing, and heightened pain sensitivity. Neuroinflammation is a recognised mechanism in conditions ranging from post-viral syndromes to autoimmunity and metabolic dysfunction, and it is frequently present as a contributing factor in patients presenting with complex neurological and cognitive complaints.

    We assess systemic and neurological inflammatory burden as part of our brain health evaluation and develop targeted anti-inflammatory strategies based on the specific drivers identified through testing.

  5. 05

    Sleep and Neurological Resilience

    Sleep is the primary mechanism by which the brain clears metabolic waste, consolidates memory, regulates mood, and restores neurological function. Chronic sleep disruption, whether driven by hormonal fluctuation, cortisol dysregulation, sleep apnoea, or other causes, has measurable and cumulative effects on cognitive performance, emotional regulation, and long-term neurological health. Sleep is assessed and addressed as an integral component of every brain health programme at The Schoeman Clinic.

Diagnosis

How We Assess Neurophysiology and Hormonal Brain

Health Assessment begins with a comprehensive clinical consultation with your doctor, covering the full history of your neurological and cognitive symptoms, their relationship to your hormonal cycle or life stage, your sleep patterns, your stress history, and any previous investigations or treatments.

Neurohormonal blood panel testing may include oestradiol, progesterone, testosterone, SHBG, cortisol, DHEA-S, thyroid function (TSH, free T3, free T4, and thyroid antibodies), fasting insulin, HbA1c, inflammatory markers, homocysteine, vitamin D, B12, folate, ferritin, and omega-3 index. Testing is conducted through The Doctors Laboratory (TDL).

Advanced functional testing through our Diagnostics and Supportive Services may be recommended where the clinical picture warrants it. This may include the Organic Acids Test (OAT), which assesses neurotransmitter metabolism, mitochondrial function, and nutritional sufficiency; gut microbiome analysis through the GI360 test, reflecting the direct influence of the gut-brain axis on neurological health; and environmental toxin testing where exposure is suspected.

Where neurodevelopmental assessment is indicated, referral to Dr Niraj Singh is arranged. Where advanced neurological investigation or brain imaging is required, we coordinate appropriate specialist referral.

Treatment

Our Approach to Hormonal Brain Health Treatment

  1. 01

    Neurohormonal Optimisation

    The most impactful intervention available for hormonally mediated neurological and cognitive symptoms is often hormonal optimisation itself. Schoeman uses her advanced training in bioidentical hormone therapy through WorldLink Medical and the Marion Gluck Training Academy to restore oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone, and thyroid hormones to levels that support optimal brain function. For many patients, this produces significant and often rapid improvement in cognitive clarity, mood, and neurological resilience.

  2. 02

    Nutritional and Metabolic Brain Support

    The brain has exceptional metabolic demands, and its function is directly dependent on an adequate supply of glucose, ketones, oxygen, and a broad range of micronutrients. Nutritional deficiencies in B12, folate, vitamin D, omega-3 fatty acids, magnesium, zinc, and iron are all associated with cognitive impairment and mood disturbance. Metabolic dysfunction including insulin resistance impairs neuronal energy supply and is one of the most significant modifiable risk factors for cognitive decline. These are assessed and addressed through targeted nutritional and metabolic prescribing.

  3. 03

    Neuroinflammation Management

    Systemic and neuroinflammatory burden is addressed through a personalised anti-inflammatory protocol informed by your test results, which may include dietary anti-inflammatory strategies, targeted supplementation, gut health restoration, and hormone optimisation.

  4. 04

    Mind-Body and Stress Physiology

    Chronic stress and HPA axis dysregulation have direct neurological consequences, impairing hippocampal function, disrupting sleep architecture, and accelerating cognitive ageing. Stress physiology is assessed and addressed as a clinical priority within the brain health programme.

  5. 05

    Specialist Referral Coordination

    Where formal neurodevelopmental assessment for ADHD or autism spectrum conditions is required, we refer to Dr Niraj Singh, a specialist Neurodevelopmental Psychiatrist. Where advanced neurological investigation is indicated, we coordinate appropriate specialist referral through our clinical network.

Why us

Why Choose The Schoeman Clinic for Hormonal Brain

Health? The Schoeman Clinic is one of a small number of clinical settings in the UK where the hormonal dimension of cognitive and neurological symptoms is assessed with the same rigour as a psychiatric or neurological presentation. Our approach recognises that the brain does not function in isolation from the endocrine, metabolic, and gastrointestinal systems, and that treating cognitive symptoms without investigating their hormonal and biological substrate leaves the most impactful levers of improvement entirely untouched.

Your doctor's combined expertise in general practice, functional medicine, and specialist hormonal therapy gives them the clinical breadth to investigate neurological and cognitive presentations comprehensively, to identify and treat the underlying drivers, and to coordinate specialist referral where the picture extends beyond the hormonal and functional medicine remit of the clinic.

The Schoeman Clinic is CQC-registered and adheres to NICE guidelines, IFM frameworks, WorldLink Medical protocols, and GMC standards throughout all patient care.

Questions

Frequently asked questions

Yes, directly and significantly. Oestrogen, testosterone, thyroid hormones, cortisol, and insulin all have measurable effects on brain function, including attention, memory, processing speed, and mood regulation. Fluctuations or deficiencies in any of these hormones produce neurological symptoms that are biological in origin, not psychological. This is well-established in the scientific literature and central to the clinical approach at The Schoeman Clinic.
Possibly, particularly if you are female and approaching or in perimenopause. The emergence or worsening of attention difficulties, impulsivity, and executive dysfunction during hormonal transition is a recognised clinical phenomenon related to declining oestrogen's effect on dopamine signalling. A thorough hormonal assessment is an important part of understanding whether this is a neurodevelopmental condition, a hormonally mediated presentation, or a combination of both. Where formal neurodevelopmental assessment is required, we refer to our specialist partner Dr Niraj Singh.
The gut and the brain are in constant bidirectional communication through a network of neural, hormonal, and immune pathways collectively referred to as the gut-brain axis. The gut microbiome produces neurotransmitters including serotonin and GABA, regulates immune function, influences systemic inflammation, and affects the availability of nutrients essential to brain function. Gut dysbiosis and intestinal permeability can have direct neurological consequences, contributing to mood disorders, cognitive impairment, and anxiety. Assessing and optimising gut health is therefore a meaningful component of brain health care.
A psychiatrist assesses and treats mental health conditions, primarily through psychotherapy and psychotropic medication. A neurologist investigates structural and functional neurological disease. The Schoeman Clinic addresses the hormonal, metabolic, nutritional, and inflammatory drivers of cognitive and neurological symptoms that fall within the intersection of endocrinology, functional medicine, and brain science. These three clinical perspectives are complementary rather than competing, and we coordinate with psychiatric and neurological specialists where the clinical picture requires it.
No referral is required. You may self-refer directly to The Schoeman Clinic. We recommend informing your GP of any specialist private care you are receiving.
